x.A: Glue is for ETL and data integration, not for orchestrating an event-driven application workflow.
x.B: Step Functions with EC2 instances keeps servers to manage, so it isn't serverless and has more overhead.
x.C: EventBridge invoking Lambda on a schedule isn't event-driven and doesn't coordinate multi-step workflows or state.
x.D: Step Functions state machines orchestrate Lambda functions for each workflow step. It's serverless, event-driven, and needs no servers to manage.

x.A: Transit gateways with inter-Region peering connect networks, but they don't reduce latency and packet loss for end users on the internet.
x.B: Global Accelerator supports UDP listeners and routes players over the AWS global network to the closest healthy Regional endpoint, which reduces latency and packet loss.
x.C: CloudFront doesn't support UDP traffic, since it works with HTTP and HTTPS.
x.D: VPC peering connects VPCs and doesn't optimize how end users reach the game, and UDP isn't something you turn on per VPC.

x.A: RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ on io2 Block Express gives high availability, but io2 Block Express is built for very high IOPS and costs much more than the 1,000 to 2,000 IOPS needed.
x.B: A Multi-AZ RDS for MySQL instance gives a managed, highly available database, and a 1 TB gp2 volume provides baseline IOPS of about 3,000, which covers double the peak. It costs far less than io2.
x.C: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is object storage, not a database.
x.D: Two EC2 instances in active-passive mode means managing the database yourself, which isn't fully managed.

x.A: Reducing Lambda concurrency limits throughput and would cause throttling, so more requests would fail.
x.B: RDS Proxy pools and reuses database connections, so many Lambda functions don't exhaust the database's connections. Only the connection endpoint needs to change in the code.
x.C: A larger instance accepts more connections but costs more and doesn't fix connection churn from Lambda.
x.D: Moving to DynamoDB would require rewriting the data layer and the code.

x.A: Lambda has a 15 minute limit and a maximum of 10 GB memory and 6 vCPUs, so it can't match 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory.
x.B: Fargate tasks have a maximum of 16 vCPUs and 120 GB of memory, so they can't match 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB.
x.C: Lightsail instances are limited in size and aren't meant for large batch computing.
x.D: AWS Batch on EC2 can launch large instances with 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory, runs the job on demand, and manages the scheduling and scaling with little operational work.

x.A: Deep Archive takes hours to retrieve data, so it isn't immediately accessible.
x.B: Standard-IA keeps data in multiple AZs with immediate access and a lower storage price for rarely accessed data, so it keeps the same availability and resiliency.
x.C: One Zone-IA stores data in one AZ, so it reduces availability and resiliency.
x.D: Moving immediately to One Zone-IA reduces resiliency and also affects data that is still frequently accessed in the first 30 days.

x.A: S3 stores the static files durably and highly available, and CloudFront caches them at the edge for fast delivery.
x.B: ElastiCache isn't an edge cache and can't serve static files at the edge.
x.C: EFS uses NFS and isn't supported on Windows Server instances.
x.D: FSx for Windows File Server provides highly available SMB shared storage that the Windows instances can mount to share the server-side code.
x.E: An EBS volume attaches to one instance (apart from Multi-Attach) and is limited to one AZ, so it can't be shared across the fleet.

x.A: Processing images on an EC2 instance means managing servers and scaling, and a single instance can't handle thousands of images per second.
x.B: Origin request policies only control which headers, cookies, and query strings are forwarded to the origin. They can't resize images.
x.C: A Lambda@Edge function can resize images and pick the right format for each client at CloudFront edge locations, with no servers to manage and automatic scaling.
x.D: Response headers policies only add or change headers in responses. They can't process images.

x.A: You don't associate an ACM certificate with S3. S3 already supports HTTPS, so this is not a valid step.
x.B: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3, so the compliance team can't administer the key.
x.C: The aws:SecureTransport condition forces TLS for data in transit, and SSE-KMS with a customer managed key encrypts data at rest and lets the compliance team administer the key.
x.D: Macie discovers sensitive data and doesn't encrypt it, and it doesn't give the team control of the encryption key.

x.A: An API key is for authorization and usage plans and doesn't change the network path the calls take.
x.B: An interface VPC endpoint for API Gateway lets resources in the VPC call private APIs through the VPC, with no code changes needed other than using the endpoint.
x.C: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, not for API Gateway.
x.D: Adding an SQS queue between the APIs changes the design and code and isn't about network routing.

x.A: RDS can't deliver sub-millisecond reads, and a custom export script adds operational work.
x.B: S3 isn't built for sub-millisecond reads for the game.
x.C: DynamoDB with DAX gives microsecond reads, DynamoDB table export sends the data to S3 without custom code, and Athena runs one-time queries. All are managed services.
x.D: DynamoDB alone doesn't give sub-millisecond reads like DAX, and the Kinesis streaming setup adds more components to manage.

x.A: A DynamoDB partition key doesn't preserve the order in which messages are received.
x.B: A Kinesis data stream preserves order within a shard, and using the payment ID as the partition key puts all messages for a payment in the same shard in order.
x.C: Memcached is a cache and doesn't keep messages in order.
x.D: A standard SQS queue doesn't guarantee order, and a message attribute doesn't change that.
x.E: An SQS FIFO queue keeps messages in order within a message group, so using the payment ID as the group ID keeps each payment's messages in order.

x.A: EventBridge doesn't guarantee the order of events.
x.B: SNS FIFO topics guarantee ordering and can fan out the events to multiple subscribers at the same time, such as the leaderboard, matchmaking, and authentication services.
x.C: SNS standard topics deliver at least once with best-effort ordering.
x.D: An SQS FIFO queue keeps order, but each message is read by a single consumer, so it can't send each event to several services concurrently by itself.

x.A: The default key policy doesn't restrict usage to authorized principals, and the SSE isn't using a customer managed key.
x.B: This covers SNS encryption at rest but not encryption in transit, and the question asks for both.
x.C: Using the default key policy doesn't restrict the key to authorized principals.
x.D: SSE with a customer managed KMS key and a key policy that restricts use to authorized principals protects data at rest, and a queue policy condition that requires TLS protects data in transit.
x.E: This sets the SQS key restriction with an IAM policy only. KMS requires the key policy to allow it, so the key policy is the proper control.

x.A: Read replicas replicate changes, including the accidental edits, so they can't restore an earlier state.
x.B: Manual snapshots capture a single moment in time and don't allow restoring to any point within 30 days.
x.C: Automated backups with point-in-time recovery, with a retention period of up to 35 days, allow restoring to any second, including 5 minutes before the change.
x.D: Multi-AZ replicates changes to a standby for availability, including the accidental edits.

x.A: Caching and throttling affect performance and rate limits, not who can access premium content.
x.B: WAF can't tell which Cognito users have a subscription, since it filters by request attributes like IP or headers.
x.C: Fine-grained IAM permissions on the DynamoDB table can limit access based on the user's identity through Cognito, so only subscribers can read premium content, with the least overhead.
x.D: API keys and usage plans manage throttling and quotas for clients and are not meant for user entitlement.

x.A: Global Accelerator supports UDP and can use NLBs as endpoints. An NLB can address on-premises targets by IP, so the application stays on premises while users get the best path and automatic failover.
x.B: An ALB handles HTTP and HTTPS only, so it can't carry the UDP application.
x.C: CloudFront doesn't support UDP traffic.
x.D: ALBs and CloudFront don't support UDP, so this fails.

x.A: An account password policy applies to all IAM users and sets complexity requirements and a password expiration period.
x.B: Password policies are set once for the account, not for each individual IAM user.
x.C: Third-party software isn't needed when IAM has a password policy feature.
x.D: A CloudWatch rule on user creation can't set password requirements, and it needs custom code.

x.A: AWS Batch runs the tasks as jobs in containers on managed compute that scales, regardless of the programming language, and EventBridge schedules them. This needs little operational effort.
x.B: App Runner is for web applications and APIs, not for scheduled batch tasks.
x.C: Lambda has a 15 minute limit, so 1-hour tasks can't run there, and tasks in different languages may not be supported.
x.D: Copies of the instance in an Auto Scaling group don't distribute the tasks, and you still manage the instances.

x.A: A NAT instance is self-managed and needs patching and failover, so it isn't a managed solution.
x.B: A NAT instance in a private subnet has no route to the internet, and it's still self-managed.
x.C: A NAT gateway is a managed service. Placed in a public subnet with the private subnets' default routes pointing to it, the instances reach the license server without being exposed to inbound internet traffic.
x.D: A NAT gateway in a private subnet can't reach the internet, because it needs to be in a public subnet.

x.A: A Kubernetes plugin would need to be set up and maintained, which adds operational overhead.
x.B: Encrypting existing volumes after creation is manual, and the volumes can't be encrypted in place.
x.C: Turning on EBS encryption by default with the customer managed key makes every new EBS volume in the Region, including the managed node group's volumes, encrypted automatically.
x.D: The EKS cluster role needs permission to use the customer managed key so that EBS volumes for the nodes can be created and used with it.
x.E: A KMS key can't be stored as a Kubernetes secret and used to encrypt EBS volumes.

x.A: Storing high-resolution images in an Oracle database on RDS is expensive and doesn't scale well for tens of thousands of updates every few minutes.
x.B: S3 stores the large images cheaply and scales, and DynamoDB maps the geographic code to the image URL with high scalability and availability for the frequent updates.
x.C: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so it can't hold high-resolution images.
x.D: A relational Oracle table for URLs on RDS costs more and scales worse than DynamoDB for this key-value access pattern.

x.A: Intelligent-Tiering is a good choice because access patterns vary. Data is read each morning and quarterly, and it needs to stay available with no delay. A lifecycle rule moves objects to Deep Archive after 1 year.
x.B: You can't configure Intelligent-Tiering itself to move objects to Glacier Deep Archive after a fixed year. Its archive access tiers work on days without access, and a lifecycle policy is the way to set it.
x.C: Standard-IA has retrieval fees, which would be high when the company retrains models with 30 days and 12 months of data.
x.D: Moving to Standard-IA after 30 days adds retrieval fees for the quarterly analysis that uses the previous 12 months, and with trillions of small objects the transitions would be costly.

x.A: Three Site-to-Site VPNs go over the internet, so the throughput and latency aren't consistent for hundreds of GB of data, and the VPCs can't talk to each other through them.
x.B: Third-party appliances in every VPC add cost and management, and the VPN is internet-based.
x.C: Three Direct Connect connections are costly, and it doesn't provide VPC to VPC communication by itself.
x.D: One Direct Connect connection gives consistent low-latency transfer to the data center, and a transit gateway connects the three VPCs to each other and to the Direct Connect connection. It's the most cost-effective.

x.A: Step Functions combines Lambda functions into serverless workflows, supports manual approval steps, and can orchestrate EC2, containers, and on-premises services. It's a managed service with little overhead.
x.B: Glue is for ETL jobs and isn't a general workflow orchestrator for approvals.
x.C: SQS passes messages between components and doesn't orchestrate multi-step workflows with approvals.
x.D: Lambda and EventBridge events can be wired together, but you must build the orchestration and state tracking yourself, which means more work.
